transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Time: 11:00 AM ET
Duration: ~45 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Garcia (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (CISO - Horizon), Priya Patel (DevOps), Marcus Lee (Compliance)

Summary: quick security review focused on audit logs and admin activity. Customer wants to confirm what is captured, export options (S3, syslog, streaming), retention controls, encryption/KMS handling, and who can access logs. Discussed SOC2 alignment, RBAC visibility, redaction and PII handling, SIEM integration. Next steps agreed: share SOC2 artifacts, sample log exports, schedule SIEM integration call.

Topics: audit-log schema, admin events captured, export and streaming options, retention and purge, encryption and KMS, data residency, RBAC on logs, SOC 2 evidence.

Transcript body:
00:00 Alex: hey thanks everyone for joining, appreciate you making time. quick intros?
00:06 Liam: hi liam o'connor, ciso at horizon payments. we're evaluating audit capabilities - what you capture and how we can pipe into our splunk / datadog, and retention controls, also cross-checking for SOC two.
00:17 Alex: great, i'll hand to maya for the deep bits, i'm around for any commercial or scope q's.
00:22 Maya: thanks alex. ok so high-level we capture two primary streams: audit logs (system and admin actions) and request logs (api calls, model inferences). audit logs include admin activity like user create/update, role changes, sso events, api key rotations, dedicated instance lifecycle events — deploys, rollback, model version changes, and also infra events such as node provisioning for dedicated/private.
00:45 Priya: when you say api calls, is that request payloads too? we need to know whether PII or cardholder data could end up in stored logs.
00:52 Maya: good q. by default request logs capture metadata (request id, route, model, token counts, latency, status codes). payloads are not stored in audit logs by default. we do have an optional request-logging mode customers can enable to capture request bodies for debugging; for PCI/PII-sensitive customers we recommend against enabling that and instead using streaming debug with ephemeral retention.
01:18 Marcus: can you run through the exact admin events you log? like user logins, sso failures, permission grants?
01:24 Maya: yes. list: user sign-in (sso/saml/oidc), failed auth attempts, token/api key creation and deletion, role/permission changes, mfa enrollment, console admin activity (who clicked deploy, who changed routing policies), secret rotations, key import/export events, k8s node lifecycle for private deployments, canary rollouts start/stop. we also log system alerts — e.g., policy violations or anomalous usage triggers.
01:50 Liam: is auth event detail including ip and user agent?
01:52 Maya: yes — timestamp, user id, user email (redacted if requested), ip, user agent, source region. we can also optionally include session ids and device fingerprinting on request.
02:05 Priya: how long are logs retained? we have regulators that require 7 years for some events, others shorter.
02:12 Alex: great point. default retention for audit logs in hosted tier is 90 days; for Dedicated/Private customers retention is configurable and we can offer longer retention windows (SLA + storage pricing). for enterprise we typically support retention out to multiple years via cold S3 export or your own storage integration.
02:30 Marcus: ok so can we export to our S3 bucket and keep for 7 years?
02:35 Maya: yes — we support scheduled exports to customer S3 (AES-256) or to your SIEM via syslog/CEF or Kafka connector. exports can be daily or hourly, and you manage lifecycle on your bucket for the 7-year rule. we also offer managed cold storage on request.
02:52 Liam: encryption — both at rest and in transit, and key ownership?
02:56 Maya: in transit is TLS 1.2+ across all services. at rest, logs stored in Redwood's storage are encrypted with server-side encryption; for enterprise customers we support bringing your own key (BYOK) via KMS integration — both cloud KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and HSM-backed key support for private deployments. when exporting to your S3, you can opt for SSE-KMS with your key or SSE-C.
03:20 Priya: if we use BYOK, do you see the plaintext keys?
03:23 Maya: no — keys are never exported to us. we integrate via grants/roles. for private on-prem deployments you manage the key material entirely; for hosted with BYOK we use KMS grants so Redwood can encrypt/decrypt as needed without having direct key export.
03:37 Liam: what about integrity and tamper-evidence for logs? we need assurances logs can't be altered without detection.
03:44 Maya: we support append-only storage semantics and can provide log digests/hashes on export. for high-compliance customers we can generate signed manifests for each export run, and we can stream logs to your SIEM where you maintain immutability policies.
04:00 Marcus: do you redact PII automatically or do we need to configure that?
04:05 Maya: we have two approaches: automated field-level redaction at ingestion for known sensitive fields (emails, credit card partials) and a post-ingest pipeline where you can specify additional patterns for masking. for hosted customers we can apply redaction rules on the platform side; for private/dedicated you often run the pipeline in your environment for full control. note: automated redaction uses heuristics so we recommend validation with your sample logs.
04:30 Priya: how easy to integrate with our Splunk/Datadog?
04:33 Maya: we provide native log exporters (syslog/CEF/Kafka) and an S3 export which your SIEM can ingest. we also have a webhook-based streaming API for near-real-time events. we can share a sample Splunk HEC config we use with other customers.
04:50 Liam: are admin logs accessible via the console? who can see them?
04:53 Maya: RBAC governs log access. only users with the "audit_viewer" or "admin" roles can view full logs in the console; you can scope visibility by team or project. API tokens used for exports are limited to the minimal permissions and you can rotate them. We log access to the logs themselves (so there's an audit trail of "who viewed which log export").
05:14 Marcus: do you keep an access log for exports, like a chain of custody?
05:18 Maya: yes, export events are recorded — who initiated, target destination, timestamp, manifest hash. we surface that in the audit ledger and also include it in export metadata.
05:27 Priya: is there a way to stream just admin events vs full request logs to reduce noise?
05:30 Maya: absolutely. streams are filterable — you can subscribe only to admin events, auth events, or request summary metrics. this helps with SIEM ingestion cost.
05:40 Liam: how do you handle data residency? we are EU-first and need logs to stay in eu-west region and exports to eu buckets.
05:47 Maya: we support region-scoped logging. hosted customers can choose region for storage and export endpoints; for EU residency we persist logs in our eu-west storage and exports to your eu bucket. for stricter needs we recommend Dedicated or Private so the control plane and data plane are fully in your VPC/region.
06:06 Alex: quick note on SOC 2 — our SOC 2 Type II report covers logging and monitoring controls; we'll share the latest report and the trust center link.
06:14 Liam: great. can you provide evidence like sample events or mapping to our control matrix?
06:18 Maya: yes — we can map event types to common control frameworks and provide sample logs (redacted). i'll attach a mapping doc and sample exports.
06:26 Priya: scenario: a rogue admin creates an api key and exfiltrates data. how fast do you detect and what does the alert look like?
06:33 Maya: we have anomaly detection rules (spike in token usage, new token created + large bulk downloads). these generate alerts and produce a mini-incident log with related events (token create, subsequent requests, target endpoints). you can route alerts to PagerDuty, Slack, or SIEM. detection is near-real-time depending on stream configuration.
06:54 Marcus: retention rules again — can they be per-tenant, per-project, per-log-type?
06:59 Maya: yes — retention policies are configurable at the project or team level. you can set different windows for admin logs vs request logs vs debug captures. deletion is a soft+hard process: soft-delete for 30 days before permanent purge unless you have archival exports.
07:17 Liam: what about legal holds? sometimes compliance needs holds on records during investigations.
07:22 Maya: we support legal hold flags that suspend automatic purge for specified datasets and generate an audit trail for the hold action. holds can be applied via API or console and require an admin role.
07:33 Priya: who has access to raw logs in your hosted environment? internal redwood staff?
07:37 Maya: minimal. access is limited to oncall and SRE with just-in-time access workflows, annotated access tickets, and we log internal access. for higher confidentiality customers we recommend Private/Dedicated so internal access is minimized.
07:51 Liam: will you provide a SOC 2 bridge letter or evidence for our auditors?
07:55 Alex: yes we provide SOC 2 report and can provide a security questionnaire + bridge if needed — will coordinate with legal.
08:03 Marcus: are there SLAs around export delivery?
08:07 Maya: for hosted daily exports there is best-effort; for Dedicated/Enterprise we have contractual SLAs for export success/failures and retries, we also offer streaming with ack semantics for guaranteed delivery.
08:20 Priya: about API key rotation — can rotation be forced on a schedule and do you surface expiring keys to admins?
08:27 Maya: yes to both — policies can enforce rotation windows and notify owners before expiry; we also have bulk-rotate endpoints for orgs.
08:35 Liam: any gotchas for PCI environments?
08:38 Maya: avoid request-body capture, use dedicated/private with BYOK and strict retention/export policies. we can provide a checklist for PCI scope reduction.
08:50 Alex: ok i want to recap next steps — i'll send SOC 2 and whitepaper, maya will send sample logs and mapping doc, priya will confirm SPI/siem endpoints and internal contact, and marcus will send retention/regulatory windows.
09:03 Liam: sounds good. appreciate the level of detail, helps our auditors.
09:07 Maya: cool; i'll follow up with the sample exports and a proposed plan for the SIEM integration.
09:12 Alex: thanks everyone — we'll get those artifacts over this week and set up the technical follow-up.

End of meeting.
